newsitem.title: THAILAND: King Bhumibol appoints Chavalit Thailand PM.
newsitem.headline: King Bhumibol appoints Chavalit Thailand PM.

text.p: King Bhumibol Adulyadej on Monday appointed Chavalit Yongchaiyudh as Thailand's 22nd prime minister, eight days after the former army chief's New Aspiration Party (NAP) won a general election.
The Thai monarch issued a royal decree naming Chavalit prime minister after he was nominated by parliament president Wan Muhamad Nor Matha.

"General Chavalit Yongchaiyudh is considered by His Majesty the King as the suitable person to be entrusted with the job of prime minister...His Majesty the King hereby appoints General Chavalit Yongchaiyudh as prime minister..." said Wan Muhamad, reading from the royal decree.
Chavalit, dressed in a white civil servant's uniform, kneeled in front of a portrait of the king to receive the decree.
He and his cabinet are expected to be officially sworn in by the king on December 1, caretaker minister attached to the prime minister's office Pokin Polakun said.

Chavalit, 64, is expected to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton on Tuesday. Clinton was due to arrive in Bangkok later on Monday for an official visit after attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit in the Philippines.
An aide said Chavalit, who was receiving a number of well-wishers at his home, would not be making any immediate statement about his appointment.

The NAP clinched a razor thin two-seat victory over rival Democrat Party in the November 17 poll by capturing 125 of the 393 seats in the lower House of Representatives. It formed a six-member coalition with a comfortable majority of 221 seats.

One of Chavalit's immediate tasks after his appointment is to finalise his cabinet. The NAP and its major partner, the 52-seat Chart Pattana Party (CPP), have held intense negotiations over how to share out key economic portfolios.

Chavalit pledged during his campaign that he would recruit a "dream team" of non-elected economic experts, led by former banker Amnuay Viravan, to help revive Thailand's sluggish economy which is projected to grow at its slowest pace in 10 years in 1996.
The CPP, led by former premier Chatichai Choonhavan, has demanded control of key economic ministries like communications and transport, industry and foreign affairs.

Chavalit's premiership culminated a gamble made six years ago when he became the first army commander-in-chief to take an unprecedented move of leaving his top military job voluntarily to enter politics before his mandatory retirement at age 60.
"He has finally made it. His rise to the top is no surprise judging from his determination to take the road that he has travelled," said Songglod Bhichaikul of United Securities Plc.
It took Chavalit three national elections to realise his goal. The bespectacled politician settled for positions as deputy premier, defence and interior minister in previous elected governments.

The former general first rose to national prominence in the early 1980s when, as army chief of staff, he was regarded as a strategist responsible for a government policy to win over Thai communists by persuading them to end a 20-year armed insurgency against the Bangkok government.
He built his military career mostly in northeastern Thailand which became the NAP's stronghold in the November 17 poll in which it won more than half the region's parliamentary seats.

Chavalit's critics said the NAP, the best financed among the political parties through its extensive business connections, managed to beat the Democrats of former premier Chuan Leekpai in the election partly by using campaign money to buy votes. NAP leaders have denied the allegation.
Thailand's independent Pollwatch called the last poll the dirtiest and most violent election in the country's history.
